title: Sharp qutrit discrimination and unavoidable correlation overcounting for complementary measurements
shortTitle: Complementary measurements: a sharp 8/3 for qutrits, and no safe choice from n = 4
oneLine: Two complementary measurements on a qutrit can score at most 8/3 (out of a trivial 4) when telling two orthogonal states apart, proved by an exact certificate with every best case identified; and for a qubit paired with a system of dimension n ≥ 4, every choice of complementary measurements is fooled by some unentangled state (previously known only from n = 164).
abstract: Two parties share a quantum system and each can measure in one of two complementary bases, as with position and momentum. In 2014 Schneeloch, Broadbent and Howell proposed that the classical correlations seen in the two resulting outcome tables never add up to more than the total quantum correlation of the shared state, the complementary quantum correlation (CQC) inequality. In 2026 it was refuted in most dimensions by public code repositories (O'Connor; AlperTheKing), by Wang, Wang and Chen and by Qian; it holds for two qubits, and the qubit–qutrit case is open. This candidate settles two follow-up questions. First, for a qutrit and any pair of complementary bases, the summed triangular discrimination of two orthogonal states is at most 8/3 (the trivial ceiling is 4), answering a question of Qian; every equality case is classified, and for the computational and Fourier bases they are tied to the nine Hesse SIC rays. Consequences: choosing one of the two measurements at random recovers at most two thirds of the quantum Fisher information in a two-state estimation task, and Qian's two-ray qubit–qutrit family obeys CQC with margin at least 0.1005 nats. The proof is computer-assisted: an exact rational sum-of-squares certificate checked by a standalone verifier. Second, for a qubit paired with a qudit of dimension n ≥ 4, every prescribed pair of complementary measurements admits a separable state violating CQC, with a uniform certified margin below −9/20,000,000 nats; previously this every-pair statement was known only for n ≥ 164. A related construction covers every pair when both dimensions are at least three. The full qubit–qutrit question and the sharp constant in dimension 5 remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Sharp qutrit discrimination (Theorem 2.1, computer-assisted proof): for every complementary (mutually unbiased) pair of qutrit bases and orthogonal states u, v, the summed triangular discrimination is at most 8/3, against a trivial ceiling of 4; this answers Qian's question (arXiv:2608.14806v2, Section 11(4)).

Every best case (Theorem 2.1): equality holds exactly when the two states span a plane through one vector of each basis and their difference is ±√(3/2) times the difference of those projectors; for the computational and Fourier bases these planes are tied to the nine Hesse SIC rays.

Measurement efficiency (Corollary 2.2): choosing one of two complementary qutrit settings at random recovers at most 2/3 of the quantum Fisher information when estimating the weight of a two-state mixture; the two-ray qubit–qutrit CQC gap rises from 0.0120 to at least 0.1005 nats (Corollary 3.3).

No safe choice from n = 4 (Theorem 4.1, proof with exact margins): for a qubit with a qudit of dimension n ≥ 4 and every prescribed pair of complementary measurements, some separable state violates CQC, with a uniform margin below −9/20,000,000 nats (−1.058 × 10⁻⁴ at n = 4); previously every-pair failure was known only for n ≥ 164.

Both dimensions at least three (Theorem 4.7): every prescribed pair admits a separable violation with a dimension-free margin, extending an earlier, unchecked every-pair statement for equal dimensions by O'Connor. The full qubit–qutrit question remains open.

narration: Can two quantum measurements be trusted to count correlation? An Evidence Press briefing. Some quantum measurements are complementary, like position and momentum: if one gives a predictable answer, the other cannot. In 2014, Schneeloch, Broadbent and Howell proposed that if two parties each make two complementary measurements on a shared system, the correlations in their two tables of results can never add up to more than the total correlation in the system. That would make two tables a cheap, guaranteed lower bound. In 2026 the idea was shown to fail in most dimensions, first in public code repositories by Ethan O'Connor and by AlperTheKing, then by Wang, Wang and Chen, and by Qian. This paper answers two follow-up questions. The first concerns a three-level system, a qutrit. How well can two complementary measurements tell two perfectly distinguishable qutrit states apart? On a natural score where four is a trivial ceiling, the paper proves that the best possible score is exactly eight thirds, and it finds every case where that best score is reached, linked to a famous symmetric arrangement called the Hesse configuration. One consequence: measuring this way recovers at most two thirds of the available information in a simple estimation task. The proof is computer-assisted: an exact certificate in whole-number fractions, checked by a short program that anyone can rerun. The second result concerns a qubit paired with a system of dimension four or more. There, every choice of complementary measurements is fooled by some unentangled state. Before, this was known only from dimension one hundred and sixty-four. The violations are tiny, so this is a structural limit, not an experimental one. The question for a qubit paired with a qutrit stays open, as does the exact best score in dimension five. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the fourth of November twenty twenty-six, its paper, certificate and code are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Schneeloch, Broadbent and Howell (2014). Uncertainty relation for mutual information. Physical Review A. Proposed the complementary quantum correlation (CQC) inequality studied here.
Berta, Christandl, Colbeck, Renes and Renner (2010). The uncertainty principle in the presence of quantum memory. Nature Physics. Proved, state-independent entropic bounds that remain valid tools.
Coles, Berta, Tomamichel and Wehner (2017). Entropic uncertainty relations and their applications. Reviews of Modern Physics. Background on complementary measurements.

Wootters and Fields (1989). Optimal state-determination by mutually unbiased measurements. Annals of Physics. Mutually unbiased measurements are optimal for full state determination; Corollary 2.2 quantifies their cost for one known pair of states.

OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro (Zenodo creator; repository owner E. O'Connor) (2026). Exact qutrit counterexample to the CQC conjecture. Zenodo, version v1.1.1. Early exact qutrit counterexample and an earlier, unchecked every-pair statement for equal dimensions, credited in the paper.
AlperTheKing (2026). cqc-counterexample: exact qutrit counterexample to the complementary-quantum-correlation conjecture. GitHub repository. Early exact qutrit counterexample.

Wang, Wang and Chen (2026). When complementary measurements count the same classical bit twice: counterexamples to CQC, ECQC, and complementarity-based certification. arXiv:2608.03828v3. Counterexamples in every dimension at least three.
Wang, Wang and Chen (2026). Complementary quantum correlations are universal for qubits. arXiv:2608.04916v1. CQC holds for two qubits.

Qian (2026). Separable counterexamples to complementary quantum correlations, and why random search missed them. arXiv:2608.14806v2. Posed the sharp qutrit question (Section 11(4)), gave the frame reduction and the every-pair result for n ≥ 164.
Iqbal (2026). On the CQC conjecture: a sufficient condition and an extension. Quantum Information Processing. Earlier sufficient conditions for CQC.
Tadej and Życzkowski (2006). A Concise Guide to Complex Hadamard Matrices. Open Systems & Information Dynamics. Classification used to reduce every qutrit complementary pair to the Fourier pair.
Stacey (2016). SIC-POVMs and Compatibility among Quantum States. Mathematics. The Hesse SIC geometry of the equality cases.
